rows.explanation: It calls every person altogether vanity even at the best estate, closely matching the ayah's universal judgment of human loss.
It says human hearts are full of evil and madness before death, joining universal corruption to a doomed end.
It says death passed upon all men because all sinned, making human ruin universal and mortal.
It says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, directly portraying universal human failure.
It says Jews and Gentiles alike are all under sin, matching mankind's shared adverse condition.
It says Scripture has concluded all under sin, a direct verdict of universal human bondage.
It says all have turned aside and none does good, a universal verdict of human moral failure.
It says all have gone aside and none does good, repeating the universal indictment of mankind.
It says no one is righteous, directly expressing an all-human deficit before God.
It says all have gone out of the way and none does good, stating universal human deviation.
It depicts the whole world as lying in wickedness, a direct picture of humanity in a ruinous condition.
It concludes that every person is vanity, reinforcing the same universal futility.
It says the sons of men share the beasts' mortality and that all is vanity, closely paralleling human loss.
It says a human being does not endure and is like beasts that perish, matching loss as the human lot.
It says no living person can be justified before God, presenting universal human inability to stand.
It says no just person on earth does good without sin, a direct universal qualification of mankind.
Its second clause declares a free gift unto justification of life for all men, answering universal condemnation with life.
It promises that God will swallow up death in victory and wipe tears from all faces, reversing ultimate human ruin.
God says the imagination of the human heart is evil from youth, a generic diagnosis underlying mankind's loss.
It portrays God returning man to destruction, a direct but mortality-focused parallel.
It calls man like vanity and his days a passing shadow, a partial parallel in human transience.
It says the honored person without understanding is like beasts that perish, a closely related but qualified loss verdict.
It describes man born of woman as few of days and full of trouble, matching the ayah's adverse human condition.
Qoheleth finds his labor vanity with no profit under the sun, employing the same loss-and-no-gain judgment.
It says a person leaves as naked as he came and carries nothing away from labor, an economic image of human loss.
It says the people are grass that withers, paralleling the ayah through universal human perishability.
It says all flesh is grass that withers, directly extending the image of human transience.
It says all its speakers have gone astray like sheep, a close collective image of humanity's lost condition.
It says the collective speakers are all unclean and their iniquities carry them away, a close portrait of moral ruin.
It says people are appointed once to die and then face judgment, a universal mortality-and-accountability parallel.
Its warning that gaining the world while losing one's soul brings no profit directly uses the same ultimate-loss logic.
It warns that gaining the whole world cannot compensate for losing one's soul, directly paralleling loss.
It asks what profit comes from gaining the world while losing oneself or being cast away, an especially close loss image.
It warns that many enter the broad way leading to destruction, a qualified version of the human-loss verdict.
It warns its hearers that unless they repent, all will perish, giving a conditional form of the loss verdict.
It repeats that without repentance all will perish, again framing human ruin as the default outcome.
It promises that the dead will live and arise, reversing mortal loss in a restoration oracle.
It pairs universal death in Adam with being made alive in Christ, answering loss with life in its resurrection argument.
It says death is swallowed up in victory in the resurrection, reversing the finality of loss.
It says Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light, reversing the deathward aspect of loss.
It envisions a final state with no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, the eschatological opposite of human ruin.
It says all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, a direct collective portrayal of humanity in ruin.
It says every imagination of the human heart was only evil continually, a near-total indictment of mankind in its Flood setting.
Solomon's prayer says there is no person who does not sin, directly universalizing human failure.
It likewise says there is no person who does not sin, directly universalizing human failure.
It says both low and high men are vanity and together lighter than vanity, closely matching loss across all social ranks.
It asks why all men were made in vain, directly voicing universal human futility.
It asks who could stand if God marked sins, implying that no human can escape guilt's ruin.
It asks who can claim a clean heart and freedom from sin, a universal denial of human purity.
It says God shut Jews and Gentiles alike up in unbelief, a universal adverse condition even as its purpose turns to mercy.
Qoheleth's thesis that all is vanity closely parallels the ayah's all-encompassing judgment of loss.
It repeats that all is vanity, restating the book's final verdict of futility.
Its assertion that all must die like spilled water gives a close image of irreversible human loss, though it then invokes God's restoring purpose.
It says man dies and wastes away, a direct mortality-focused parallel.
It warns that a way seeming right to a person ends in death, a closely related argument about fatal human misjudgment.
It says all human labor is for the mouth yet desire remains unfilled, a closely related image of futile striving.
It describes the human heart as deceitful and desperately wicked, a generic diagnosis of the condition behind loss.
It says the soul that sins shall die, a general moral rule expressing loss as sin's consequence.
It warns of the destruction of both soul and body in hell, a direct warning of ultimate loss.
It says the unbeliever is condemned already, a conditional but direct verdict of present ruin.
It says sin earns death, setting out a general loss-consequence even as the verse contrasts God's gift of life.
It says “we all” were by nature children of wrath like others, a collective diagnosis of human peril.
It says the outward person is perishing, a direct but believer-specific parallel answered by inner renewal.
It says all stumble in many things, a broad acknowledgment of universal human failure.
It summons all ends of the earth to look to God and be saved, an all-encompassing answer to human loss.
It calls those facing death to turn and live, directly answering loss with life.
It promises that whoever believes will not perish but have everlasting life, a conditional reversal of loss.
It promises that death, the last enemy, will be destroyed, reversing mortal ruin.
It envisions mortality swallowed up by life, a direct reversal of deathward loss.
It says God wills all people to be saved and know the truth, expressing the universal opposite aim.
It says God wills none to perish but all to come to repentance, the opposite of a universal destiny of loss.
It promises that there will be no more curse in the final city, reversing the condition of ruin.
Its picture of wages put into a bag with holes gives a concrete but Judah-specific image of loss.
